summary: The origin of the name "Senegal" is debated and no hypothesis is authoritative: the link to the Sanhaja, a Berber confederation that French calls Zenaga, is the most widespread; the Wolof explanation "sunu gaal", "our pirogue", goes back to Abbé Boilat in 1853; and both have their challengers. The Jolof Empire, the Serer kingdoms and Fouta Toro shared the territory among them. Wolof, Fulani, Serer, Jola, Mandinka and Soninké peoples carry on the griots' word.
etymology: The origin of the name "Senegal" is not established and remains disputed. The most widespread hypothesis links it to the Sanhaja, a Berber confederation of the western Sahara whom French and Portuguese name Zenaga; Théodore Monod and Raymond Mauny defend it in 1960 against the Wolof explanation. It has long been disputed. In the first edition of the Encyclopaedia of Islam, Maurice Delafosse notes that most modern authors rally to it, yet judges the connection fortuitous, and proposes another source: a kingdom of the lower valley of the river, which ancient texts name Sanghana in al-Bakri in the eleventh century, Senegany on a portolan chart of 1351, then Sanaga and Senega among fifteenth-century navigators. The Wolof explanation "sunu gaal", "our pirogue", is later and of a single origin: Abbé Boilat puts it forward in his Esquisses sénégalaises in 1853, and nothing attests to it before him. Paul Marty opposes it in 1917 with the Hassaniya term Singhane, by which the Moors designated Cayor, and holds the Berber etymologies to be fanciful. Saliou Kandji rejects them all in 2006. One question remains that these readings do not raise: what did the peoples of the river call it? In 1573, the Spanish geographer Luis del Mármol Carvajal records two answers. The Toucouleurs say Mayo, which simply means "the river" in Pulaar. The Soninke of Ngalam say Colle. Neither of these two names survived on maps, and the one that prevailed is foreign to them.
nameOriginActor: The name is first that of the river, carried by European navigators and cartographers from the fifteenth century, then extended to the territory. What they transcribed remains disputed: a Berber name, that of a kingdom of the lower valley, a Hassaniya term or a Wolof phrase, according to different authors. None of these attributions is established.

historicalNames.antiquity: The territory was inhabited by Wolof, Serer, Fula, Mandinka and Jola groups with no unified name. Regional empires (Ghana, Mali, Songhai) influenced the region.
historicalNames.middleAges: Thirteenth-sixteenth centuries: Jolof Empire (Wolof) with vassal kingdoms (Cayor, Baol, Waalo, Sine, Saloum). Fouta Toro (Fula theocracy).
historicalNames.precolonial: Wolof kingdoms (Jolof, Cayor, Baol, Waalo), Serer kingdoms (Sine, Saloum), Fula theocracy of Fouta Toro, Jola kingdoms of Casamance. Trans-Saharan trade and coastal trade.
historicalNames.colonization: Fifteenth century: first Portuguese contacts (name "Senega"). 1659: founding of Saint-Louis by the French. 1895: integration into French West Africa (AOF). The territory is called "Senegal" by the colonisers.
historicalNames.contemporary: Independence in 1960 under the name "Republic of Senegal". The official name in French is "République du Sénégal".

kingdoms.name: Jolof Empire
kingdoms.historicalRole: Powerful Wolof empire that unified several kingdoms. Trans-Saharan trade and coastal trade. Major cultural influence.

kingdoms.name: Serer kingdoms
kingdoms.historicalRole: Independent Serer kingdoms known for their resistance to Islamisation and their political organisation.

kingdoms.name: Fouta Toro
kingdoms.historicalRole: Islamised Fula theocracy, a political and religious model for the region.

kingdoms.name: French Senegal
dominantPeoples: Tous les peuples sénégalais sous administration coloniale française
kingdoms.historicalRole: French colony integrated into French West Africa (AOF). Development of Dakar as the administrative capital. Senegalese resistance and nationalist movements.

kingdoms.name: Republic of Senegal
kingdoms.historicalRole: Independence in 1960. Stable political history with multi-party democracy. A model of stability in West Africa.

majorPeoples.name: Wolof
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: The term "Wolof" is neutral and accepted.

majorPeoples.name: Peul / Fulani
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: The term "Fellata" can be pejorative. The self-given name "Fulɓe" is preferred. "Peul" and "Fulani" are accepted.

majorPeoples.name: Sérère
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: The term "Sérère" is neutral and accepted.

majorPeoples.name: Diola / Jola
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: The terms "Diola" and "Jola" are neutral and accepted. The self-given name "Joola" is preferred.

majorPeoples.name: Mandinka / Mandingue
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: The term "Mandinka" is neutral and accepted.

majorPeoples.name: Soninké
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: The term "Soninké" is neutral and accepted. "Sarakolé" is an accepted variant.

culture.culturalTraditions: Traditional music (sabar, mbalax), traditional dance, oral poetry (griot), crafts (basket weaving, pottery, weaving), traditional architecture, Senegalese wrestling
culture.dominantReligions: Islam (majority Sufi: Tijaniyya, Muridiyya), Christianity (minority), traditional beliefs (syncretism)
culture.lifestyles: Predominantly rural life, agriculture (groundnuts, millet, sorghum, rice), livestock farming (cattle, goats), fishing (coasts and rivers), trade, growing urbanisation
culture.socialOrganization: System of traditional chieftaincies, patrilineal clan structure, organisation into extended families and lineages, importance of griots (keepers of oral tradition), system of Sufi brotherhoods
culture.regionalRelations: Historical relations with the peoples of Gambia, Mauritania, Mali and Guinea. A significant diaspora in France, Italy and other Western countries.

historicalFacts.ancientPeriods: Settlement of the territory by Wolof, Serer, Fula, Mandinka and Jola groups. Influence of regional empires (Ghana, Mali, Songhai).
historicalFacts.middleAges: Development of the Jolof Empire (thirteenth-sixteenth centuries). Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum. Fula theocracy of Fouta Toro. Trans-Saharan trade and coastal trade.
historicalFacts.precolonial: Height of the Wolof and Serer kingdoms. Trade with Europeans (gold, ivory, slaves). Resistance to Islamisation among some groups (Serer).
historicalFacts.colonization: Fifteenth century: first Portuguese contacts. 1659: founding of Saint-Louis by the French. 1895: integration into French West Africa (AOF). Development of Dakar as the administrative capital. Senegalese resistance.
historicalFacts.independenceStruggle: Nationalist movements in the 1950s. Independence achieved in 1960. Léopold Sédar Senghor becomes the first president.
historicalFacts.postIndependence: First Republic (1960-1980): Senghor's presidency, political stability. Second Republic (1981-2000): presidency of Abdou Diouf. Third Republic since 2000: democratic alternation, political stability, economic development.

sources.notes: Notes that most modern authors link the name to the Sanhaja, judges this connection coincidental, and proposes a kingdom of the lower valley, Sanghana. The entry was consulted on 9 September 2026; its beginning is freely accessible, the rest is paywalled.

sources.title: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Chronique de Guinée, traduction de Léon Bourdon, édition scientifique de Théodore Monod et Raymond Mauny, IFAN, Dakar, 1960
sources.notes: Edition in which Monod and Mauny set aside the Wolof explanation in favour of the Berber connection. The printed work is verified in the catalogue of the Bibliothèque nationale de France; the passage itself has not been read, and is reported via a presentation of Saliou Kandji's book.

sources.title: P.-David Boilat, Esquisses sénégalaises, Paris, P. Bertrand, 1853
sources.notes: Earliest known formulation of the Wolof explanation "sunu gaal". The edition is verified in the catalogue of the Bibliothèque nationale de France, where the date of 1850 often cited does not correspond to any printing. The page carrying the passage has not been located in the digitised volume, so no page number is given.

sources.title: Paul Marty, Études sur l'Islam au Sénégal, Paris, Ernest Leroux, 1917, 2 volumes
sources.notes: Proposes the Hassaniya term Singhane, the Moorish name for Cayor, and sets aside the Berber etymologies. The work is verified in the catalogue of the Bibliothèque nationale de France; the passage does not appear in the only digitised volume and has not been read.

sources.title: Saliou Kandji, Sénégal n'est pas Sunugal, ou De l'étymologie du toponyme Sénégal, Presses universitaires de Dakar, 2006, 56 pages
sources.notes: Rejects both the Wolof explanation and the Berber connections. The work does not appear in the catalogue of the Bibliothèque nationale de France; title, publisher, year and pagination are taken from a press presentation.

sources.title: Présentation de « Sénégal n'est pas Sunugal », de Saliou Kandji, Seneweb
sources.notes: Unsigned presentation. It is the source of the attribution of the term Singhane to Paul Marty and of the disagreement between Monod and Mauny and Boilat. It dates the Esquisses sénégalaises to 1850, which is inaccurate.

sources.title: Luis del Mármol Carvajal, Primera parte de la descripción general de Áffrica, Grenade, René Rabut, 1573
sources.notes: Gives two names of the river among the peoples of its banks: Mayo among the Toucouleurs, Colle among the Soninke of Ngalam. The printed work is digitised by the Biblioteca Virtual del Patrimonio Bibliográfico. The passage is located in book VIII, chapter 3; it has not been read in the original, and the reference was found via the English version of Wikipedia, consulted on 9 September 2026.
